The final column gives the ML threshold φ * for equal versus unequal fitted loadings across the two blocks; its "many" entry is the limit λ 2 /(2 -λ 2 ).

4 Population Fit and the Distinction Between Traits

The minimum discrepancy in Theorem 1 provides a population benchmark for interpreting a one-factor fit. For a specified loading and test length, it identifies the trait correlations at which the fitted model meets a conventional cutoff although two traits generated the data. A cutoff boundary concerns overall fit. The threshold φ * identifies the correlation at which the factor begins to represent the two traits equally.

4.1 Cutoff Boundaries

Table 1 gives the cutoff boundaries for CFI, TLI, RMSEA and SRMR. With loadings of .70 and 4 to 16 items in total, a one-factor model meets CFI ≥ .95 when the trait correlation reaches approximately .78 to .84. The corresponding RMSEA boundary decreases from .92 to .84 as items are added. Thus, a favorable CFI does not establish that the two generating traits are identical, and disagreement between indices can occur at the population level.

All of the CFI ≥ .95 boundaries in Table 1 lie in the equal-loading regime of Theorem 1.

Consequently, these examples of favorable CFI should be distinguished from the preferential representation of one trait at lower correlations. The practical point is that an overall fit index does not by itself resolve either the dimensionality of the population or the interpretation of the fitted factor.

The closed forms for CFI, TLI and RMSEA follow by substituting F min into their definitions.

For SRMR, the fitted model reproduces the diagonal, and the remaining residuals take three values.

Hence

In the equal-loading regime, this reduces to

For φ ≥ λ 2 /(2 -λ 2 ), the limiting CFI and TLI as the number of items increases are

The indices differ because they summarize discrepancy in different ways. RMSEA divides the discrepancy by the model degrees of freedom. It decreases at rate m -1/2 for fixed loading and trait correlation, and its limit is zero.

Thus, sufficiently long tests meet a fixed positive RMSEA cutoff even when the two traits are uncorrelated. CFI and TLI compare model discrepancy with independence-model discrepancy; TLI also adjusts for degrees of freedom. At loading .70, their limiting .95 cutoff boundary is approximately .93. Finite-length boundaries need not be monotone: the TLI boundaries are .87, .85 and .86 for 4, 8 and 16 items. SRMR instead summarizes the sizes of residual correlations. It depends directly on λ 2 and has little dependence on test length once m is moderately large. It does not normalize residuals by their precision or by baseline discrepancy. It is the most permissive cutoff for the finite item counts in Table 1. For four items loading .50, SRMR is .079 at φ = 0, so two independent traits meet the .08 cutoff. Kenny and McCoach (2003) derived the symmetric-branch population CFI and TLI. The limiting expression above follows from their determinant formulas, and they also described the decline of RMSEA with test length. Shi, Lee and Maydeu-Olivares (2019) studied model-size effects numerically. Theorem 1 adds the global classification: it identifies when the symmetric expression is the minimum and supplies the asymmetric branch when it is not. The cutoff calculations therefore use the minimum over the full one-factor model.

The exact discrepancy can also be used in the conventional noncentral-χ 2 power approximation, with noncentrality N F min for sample size N under the normal-likelihood convention. This approximation is justified under regular local alternatives. Its finite-sample accuracy under fixed misspecification, near φ * and at nonregular endpoints is not established by the population formulas (Chun & Shapiro, 2009).

4.2 CFI at a Fixed Information Loss

A change in CFI need not indicate a change in the information lost by the one-factor approximation.

Fix p = 2m and the contrast signal-to-noise ratio κ -, and vary the loading along within the regime φ ≥ φ * .

Theorem 1 implies that F min , the Kullback-Leibler divergence and RMSEA are constant on this path. The baseline discrepancy increases with λ 2 , however, so CFI increases.

More explicitly, the derivative of total correlation with respect to λ 2 along this path is positive exactly when κ -< (2m -1)λ 2 /(1 -λ 2 ), a condition satisfied on the stated path with φ ≥ 0. For eight items and κ -= 1, the Kullback-Leibler divergence is .121 (half of F min = .242) and RMSEA is .110 throughout the path, whereas CFI is .62, .82, .91, .95 and .97 at loadings .5, .6, .7, .8 and .9.

At loading .5 the path meets the threshold, φ = φ * = .25. Moshagen and Auerswald (2018) showed that RMSEA and the conventional noncentral-χ 2 power approximation do not depend on loadings when discrepancy is held fixed. The calculation here gives the corresponding result for an incremental index. It also clarifies the relation to the reliability paradox: studies of that phenomenon hold the form of misspecification fixed and find that fit worsens as loadings increase (Hancock & Mueller, 2011; McNeish, An & Hancock, 2018). The direction of the loading effect depends on which feature of the population is held constant.

For heterogeneous loadings, the exact expressions need not apply. Proposition 5 in Appendix E gives an upper bound on the information lost by the best one-factor approximation.

The bound depends on the smaller eigenvalue of the trait signal after each item is scaled by its unique standard deviation.

5 Estimation Criteria and Unequal Measurement

We first vary the fitting criterion while keeping the two blocks exchangeable. We then return to ML and vary the block lengths and loadings, including loadings on both traits.

5.1 Dependence on the Fitting Criterion

The transition in Theorem 1 depends on the estimation criterion. Under unweighted least squares (ULS), it occurs at 1/p, independently of the population loading. Principal components retain the equal block-mean direction at every positive trait correlation. Thus a single population can yield an equal composite under one criterion and a factor that emphasizes one trait under another.

Theorem 2 (Unweighted least squares solution). For the population in Section 2, let be the least-squares, or MINRES, objective with free uniquenesses; the constraint

For φ > 0, every global minimizer has a common loading sign. Choose that sign to be positive. If 0 < φ < 1/(2m) = 1/p, every global minimizer is constant within blocks; after ordering the blocks, its block loadings α > β > 0 satisfy

At and above φ = 1/(2m), the positive minimizer is unique and symmetric, with

The branches coincide at

At φ = 0, either block is fitted exactly and the other has zero loadings, giving G min = m(m -1)L 2 /2.

For m ≥ 3, all retained loadings equal λ, up to their common sign. For m = 2, the retained pair is (t, L/t), L ≤ t ≤ 1, up to its common sign; these representations give the same retained-block covariance.

Appendix C gives the unrestricted proof; Online Resource 1 holds the routine algebra. The argument uses a tight relaxation to establish constant loadings within blocks, then minimizes a convex quadratic over a cone. The result characterizes global minimizers; it does not assert a complete classification of nonglobal ULS local minima.

Weighted least squares makes the source of the difference more explicit. Let w W > 0 and w C > 0 be the weights given to within-block and cross-block residual correlations, respectively, and define

Each weight is constant within its pair class.

Proposition 1 (Weighted least squares solution). For the population in Section 2, minimize G w over |l i | ≤ 1. For φ > 0, every global minimizer has a common loading sign; choose it to be positive.

If ω > (m -1)/m, the threshold is

For 0 < φ < φ ω , every global minimizer is constant within blocks; after ordering the blocks, its block loadings α > β > 0 satisfy

At and above the threshold, the positive global minimizer is unique and symmetric, with

The branches agree at l2 = L/2. If ω ≤ (m -1)/m, the positive symmetric solution is the unique global minimizer at every φ > 0.

At φ = 0, nonzero blocks may have independent signs, and the global minimizers depend on the sign of ωm -m + 1. If ω > (m -1)/m, they form the retained-block family of Theorem 2. If ω = (m -1)/m, every global minimizer is block-uniform with α 2 + β2 = L, except that when m = 2 a zero block also permits the retained-pair family of Theorem 2. If ω < (m -1)/m, both blocks are uniform and have squared loading L(m -1)/(m -1 + ωm).

Appendix C gives the unrestricted proof; Online Resource 2 holds the routine algebra and the equality analysis at φ = 0 for ω ≤ (m -1)/m. As for ULS, the result characterizes global minimizers and does not classify nonglobal local minima. Setting ω = 1 recovers the minimizers in Theorem 2 and the threshold 1/p. Reducing the relative weight on cross-block residuals lowers the threshold, and can remove the asymmetric regime altogether.

For ordinal items with common thresholds, the parameter-fitting part of WLSMV uses diagonally weighted least squares on the polychoric correlations, with thresholds estimated freely. The residual weights are the inverse asymptotic variances of the polychoric estimates. In the exchangeable population, there is one weight within blocks and one across blocks, so Proposition 1 applies with ω equal to the ratio of the within-block and cross-block asymptotic variances. Because the variances depend on φ, we evaluate the right side of (5.1) at ω(φ). Denote this value by b w (φ), including when it is nonpositive and there is no positive threshold. A positive transition satisfies φ = b w (φ).

In each design evaluated here, this equation had a single root, or none, on [0, .95]; uniqueness of the root is not established in general.

In the ordinal designs considered here, the within-block correlations are estimated more precisely and ω < 1. WLSMV therefore has a lower transition than ULS, or remains symmetric throughout the evaluated range of trait correlations. With four response categories and thresholds (-.8, 0, .8), population loading .5 gives WLSMV thresholds of .081 for four items per trait and .010 for eight. At loading .7, ω = .62 when φ = 0; for four or more items per trait this is below (m -1)/m. Across the evaluated correlation range, φ exceeds b w (φ) by at least .10, and no asymmetric WLSMV solution occurs. Changing the thresholds to (.3, 1.0, 1.7) changes the reported transition values by less than .01. Appendix C describes the calculation of the weights. These parameter-fitting results are distinct from the unscaled, scaled, and robust fit-index calculations for WLSMV (Savalei, 2021).

At loading .7, ML thresholds for tests with p = 4, 8, and 16 items are approximately .49, .41, and .37, respectively, and tend to λ 2 /(2 -λ 2 ) = .32 as the number of items increases. ULS thresholds for the same test lengths are .25, .125, and .0625 and tend to zero. The four-category WLSMV threshold is approximately .10 for p = 4; for p = 8 and 16 the fitted factor remains a composite at every evaluated correlation. The leading principal component remains in the equal block-mean direction for every φ > 0.

These differences reflect how the criteria use residual correlations. ML can reduce its discrepancy by fitting one block closely while allowing larger uniquenesses in the other. ULS weights all residual correlations equally, so this solution occurs only below φ = 1/p, which is small unless the test is very short. WLSMV weights each residual by its estimation precision. In the examples above, this favors the within-block correlations and further reduces the range in which the fitted factor emphasizes one trait.

5.2 Unequal Measurement of the Two Traits

For equally long blocks with different population loadings and 0 < φ < 1, the global ML solution is unique up to sign and favors the more strongly measured trait. A second local minimum can favor the weaker trait (Proposition 2). With different block lengths, two solutions can fit equally well at a particular correlation. We give a numerical example below.

The reduction to two fitted loadings remains valid when block sizes and population loadings differ across blocks.

Lemma 1 (Constant fitted loadings within blocks). Let block A contain m A ≥ 2 items with population loading λ A and block B contain m B ≥ 2 items with loading λ B , where 0 < λ A , λ B < 1 and 0 < φ < 1. Every local minimum of the one-factor ML discrepancy over free loadings and nonnegative uniquenesses has strictly positive uniquenesses. After a common sign change, its loadings are positive and constant within each block: α in A and β in B. The uniquenesses are 1 -α 2 and 1 -β 2 , respectively. Appendix D gives the reduction argument and the scalar equation that classifies the resulting solutions. The reduction does not require equal loadings across blocks, but it does require the population correlation structure stated in the lemma. Stated in terms of correlations, the proof covers items that are exchangeable within each block, with within-block correlations r A , r B ∈ (0, 1) and a positive cross-block correlation c satisfying c2 ≤ r A r B . With λ k = √ r k and φ = c/ √ r A r B , this is the class of the lemma together with φ = 1; it is not a wider class. It includes the common-parts and cross-loading constructions described in that appendix. Negative cross-block correlation is handled by reflecting one block. Exchangeability within blocks alone is insufficient; Appendix D.1 gives a counterexample.

At zero trait correlation, the fitted factor retains the block with the larger total correlation, and is diag(I m A , R B ).

Lemma D.1 proves both cases. At equality both covariances minimize the discrepancy (Online Resource 3, Section 2.1). When the two total correlations are equal but the block lengths differ, it remains open which of these solutions continues as the global solution for small positive φ. A retained two-item block has the same parameter nonuniqueness as in Theorem 1 (Online Resource 3, Section 2.1). For equal block sizes, the larger population loading determines which block is retained.

To describe a fitted loading pattern in the coordinates of the generating traits, define covariancematching coefficients w A and w B by where l A and l B are the fitted block loadings (α and β under Lemma 1).

The coefficients are uniquely determined for |φ| < 1. We orient the fitted factor so that w A + w B > 0, and we report the coefficient share max(w A , w B )/(w A + w B ), which is undefined when w A + w B = 0. When both coefficients are nonnegative, it lies between .5, for an equal composite, and 1, for a single trait. We call the trait with the larger coefficient the followed trait. This normalized coefficient share describes the fitted covariance pattern. It is not a proportion of explained variance or the trait share of an estimated factor score.

Proposition 2 (Equal block sizes and unequal loadings). Suppose each block contains m ≥ 2 items, 0 < λ A < λ B < 1, and 0 < φ < 1. The global minimum is unique up to a common sign. It satisfies β > α, and the trait measured by block B is the followed trait. A second local minimum, with α > β and the trait measured by block A as the followed trait, exists for some positive trait correlation if and only if

When this condition holds, there is a unique φ f ∈ (0, 1) such that the second minimum exists exactly for 0 < φ < φ f . At φ f it meets a saddle in a nondegenerate fold and ceases to be a local minimum.

If the condition fails, including equality, the global solution is the only local minimum for every

A fold is a correlation at which a local minimum meets a saddle point and both disappear.

It is nondegenerate when this collision has the generic saddle-node form; Appendix D.2 gives the conditions. Condition (5.2) states that the leading eigenvalue of block A's correlation matrix after each item is scaled by its unique standard deviation, 1 + mλ 2 A /(1 -λ 2 A ), exceeds the leading eigenvalue 1 + (m -1)λ 2 B of the omitted block's correlation matrix. Equivalently, at φ = 0 the exact fit to A alone has positive curvature in the omitted block's loading directions (Lemma D.2 in Appendix D.1). With four items per block and λ B = .8, it requires λ A > .5695. For loadings .68 and .72, the weaker-block minimum persists up to φ f = .242; for .6 and .8, it persists only up to φ f = .017. Thus the absence of nonglobal ML minima in Theorem 1 depends on the exchangeable design. It is not a general property of one-factor fitting to two traits.

The trait composition of a factor score differs from the coefficient share. A score S = g ⊤ x with weight vector g, for the item vector x, has trait part (Λ ⊤ g) ⊤ θ, where Λ is the two-factor population loading matrix and θ = (θ 1 , θ 2 ) ⊤ . Its share for trait A is therefore (Λ

For four items per trait, loading .7, and φ = .3, the followed-trait shares are .786 for the fitted factor, .750 for these scores, and .500 for the unit-weighted sum. In the exchangeable design with 0 < φ < φ * , the score share lies strictly between the other two (Appendix D.6). The six PHQ-ADS sensitivity calculations with nine and seven items and common loadings of .70 or .80 also gave this ordering numerically. When loadings differ within a block, the factor share uses block-average loadings and is an approximation.

Figure 2 shows that modest differences in measurement can produce substantial differences in trait representation. With loadings .68 and .72, the followed-trait share decreases smoothly from 1 at φ = 0 to .77 at φ = .409, the threshold of the exchangeable design with loading .70, and to .57 at φ = .9. With loadings .6 and .8, it remains above .8 even at φ = .9. The poorer local solution can be distinguished by its discrepancy: in the .68/.72 design at φ = .05, its value is 1.25, compared with .99 at the global minimum.

Sensitivity is greatest near the exchangeable threshold. If the loadings are λ -ε and λ + ε, Theorem 3 in Appendix D shows that, for fixed interior λ and small positive ε, the tilt away from equal trait representation at φ * is of order ε 1/3 . The distance between φ * and the weaker solution's fold is of order ε 2/3 . At λ = .7 with four items per block, a loading difference of .01 (ε = .005) moves the followed-trait share at φ * from .5 to approximately .68. The theorem concerns a local perturbation of the balanced design; its approximation is not uniform near loading zero or one.

Unequal block sizes introduce a further possibility. A longer block can dominate at low trait correlation even when its items have smaller loadings, and the favored block can change as the correlation increases. With two items loading .85 and three loading .75, the longer block is favored initially, whereas the shorter block is favored above φ = .758. Near φ = 1, the comparison depends on m k (m k -1){λ 2 k /(1 -λ 2 k )} 2 for blocks k = A, B. This high-correlation criterion follows from a first-order expansion at the exact fit. For the .85/.75 example, an exact Sturm and discriminant calculation establishes uniqueness on [.5, 1) and locates the crossing (Appendix D.5; Online Resource 3, Section 2.6). For 0 < φ < .5, where a worse local minimum favoring the shorter block can coexist, a computer-assisted interval-arithmetic certificate reported there (checks/unequal_example_certificate.py) shows that the discrepancy at the minimum favoring the longer block is strictly smaller than at every other positive stationary point of the reduced problem, so this minimum is the unique global solution.

A different pattern occurs with two items loading .90 and four loading .70. Numerical evaluation of the quartic places the exchange between two distinct minima at φ ≈ .326, where the share of the coefficient sum w A + w B belonging to the shorter block's trait jumps from .10 to .92 (Appendix D.5; Online Resource 3, Section 2.6). In the .85/.75 design the share crosses .5 continuously on a single global branch.

5.3 Cross-Loadings and Negative Trait Correlations

Cross-loadings change the relation between the correlation of the generating traits and the correlation relevant to the one-factor approximation. In a design with equal, mirrored cross-loadings, this change has an exact expression. The result explains why a one-factor fit can combine information from two uncorrelated traits without contradicting the single-block solution at φ = 0 in Theorem 1.

In this section, ρ denotes the correlation of the generating traits, to distinguish it from the effective correlation φ eff defined below.

Proposition 3 (Equal cross-loadings). Let each block contain m ≥ 2 items. Every item in block A has primary and secondary loadings (λ p , λ s ) on (θ 1 , θ 2 ), and every item in block B has loadings (λ s , λ p ). Suppose that the traits have unit variance and correlation ρ, and that item residuals are mutually independent, independent of the traits, and have common variance τ² > 0. Define the signal variance and the between-block signal covariance and assume σ 2 S > 0.

The standardized item correlation matrix has the exchangeable form of Section 2, with λ 2 and φ replaced by where -1 ≤ φ eff ≤ 1.

Proof. Because the residuals are independent of the traits and of each other, the common signal variance of each item is σ 2 S , and the signal covariance between blocks is σ AB . Dividing within-and between-block covariances by the common item variance τ² + σ 2 S gives the stated parameters. The identities σ

For probit latent responses, τ² = 1; when the item variance is already standardized, τ² + σ 2 S = 1, λ 2 eff = σ 2 S . Negative effective correlations require only a sign change. Reversing the signs of the items in block B maps R(λ, φ) to R(λ, -φ) and leaves each discrepancy considered here unchanged. For λ p > 0 and ρ = 0, write r = λ s /λ p for the secondary-to-primary slope ratio. Then φ eff = 2r/(1 + r 2 ). Table 2 gives the smallest nonnegative ratio for which the Gaussian one-factor ML approximation has equal block loadings. Across these designs, ratios from .08 to .22 suffice.

Thus, modest cross-loadings can place uncorrelated generating traits in the equal-loading regime. This is a result for the stated latent-response populations; it does not establish the prevalence of such cross-loadings in substantive applications.

The distinction matters when interpreting simulation studies that fit unidimensional IRT models to two-dimensional data. A unidimensional approximation can reflect both generating traits when items have compensatory cross-loadings, whereas exact simple structure permits a single-block solution at zero trait correlation. The Gaussian mapping provides a mechanism that can produce these different findings. It does not by itself identify the likelihood solution in every IRT design.

For example, Strachan et al. (2022) examined primary slopes from 1.2 to 1.6 and secondary slopes from .2 to .6, with a representative ratio of approximately .29. For 20 items per block, take representative logistic slopes 1.4 and .4 and divide both by 1.702 to obtain a Gaussian probit analogue. The equal-cross-loading mapping then gives the effective correlations and ML thresholds in the second and third columns of Table 3. At trait correlations 0, -.4 and -.8, they place the analogue in the equal-loading, unequal-loading and bipolar regimes, respectively. At the last value, a composite constrained to have nonnegative weights cannot represent the bipolar direction. This offers a possible explanation for the instability of their nonnegative composite approximation at negative correlations.

Heterogeneous cross-loadings produced the same qualitative regimes. We drew slopes for 20 items per trait from the ranges of Strachan et al. (2022), primary slopes from U (1.2, 1.6) and secondary slopes from U (.2, .6), and divided them by 1.702 to convert the logistic metric. A one-factor model was fitted by ML to the latent-response correlation matrix, with all parameters free and 25 random starts. The best solution found was approximately balanced at ρ = .8, .4 and 0, favored block B at ρ = -.4, and formed a bipolar contrast at ρ = -.8 (Table 3). The pattern is consistent with the effective-correlation result, but the mapping is approximate because slopes vary within blocks. These calculations concern a Gaussian latent-response analogue; they do not evaluate binary responses fitted by marginal ML. Appendix H treats binary responses numerically.

6 Finite-Sample Behavior

We examined how closely sample fit indices followed their population values under each estimator.

We also examined whether changing the item order or starting values changed which one-factor solution lavaan returned. Appendix G gives the simulation protocol and Appendix H reports separate population calculations for binary responses.

The archived study (Tomašević, 2026a) crossed 92 populations, four sample sizes (250, 500, 1,000 and 2,000), and three response formats (continuous, and four categories with symmetric or skewed thresholds), yielding 1,104 cells: exchangeable blocks of 4 or 8 items per trait with loading .5 or .7 (Design A), two four-item blocks with loadings .68 and .72 or .60 and .80 (Design B), and the PHQ-ADS layout of 9 and 7 items with loading .75 (Design C). Trait correlations ran from 0 to .9 in steps of .1, plus .01, .24 and .409 in Design B (.01 and .24 lie just below the population folds .017 and .242) and further design-specific values in Designs A and C. One-factor models were fitted in lavaan (Rosseel, 2012) by ML, ULS, WLSMV and ML on ordinal scores; in Designs B and C at N = 500 and 2,000, the ML fits also used both default item orders and 20 random starts (Appendix G.1). A solution group is higher-objective when its lavaan objective exceeds that of the best solution found, the group with the lowest observed objective, by more than 10 -7 ; these classifications do not establish sample stationarity or global optimality.

6.1 Fit Indices

Sample fit indices generally followed their population references (best-found multistart solutions, checked against the closed forms where available), although the agreement depended on the solution returned. In Designs A and C, the correlation at which half the samples met CFI ≥ .95 or RMSEA ≤ .06 was within .03 of the population crossing point at every sample size, whereas for SRMR at N = 250 the correlation required to pass the cutoff was up to .11 higher than the population value (Appendix G.4). For ordinal items, the population reference values of robust WLSMV CFI, TLI and RMSEA (Savalei, 2021) were within .004 of the continuous-ML population values across the evaluated populations with φ ≥ .7, a numerical finding for these designs, whereas lavaan's unscaled and scaled WLSMV indices were more lenient near the cutoffs. The population agreement did not eliminate differences in small-sample cutoff-passing rates: in the PHQ-ADS layout at N = 250 and φ = .912, robust WLSMV CFI passed less often than continuous-ML CFI, 83% against 99%.

6.2 Loading Imbalance and Item Order

The estimators differed substantially in the magnitude of sample loading imbalance (Figure 3). With four items per trait, loading .7 and N = 2,000, mean |C mag | under ML declined from .930 at φ = 0 to .139 at the grid point .409 near φ * and .048 at .5. Under ULS, it was .317 at the ULS population threshold 1/p = .125, and WLSMV on symmetric categories produced much less imbalance, .102 at φ = 0. Thus, the population thresholds locate changes in the population solution, but sample imbalance remains positive on both sides (Appendix G.5).

In Design A, the two blocks had the same number of items and the same population loading.

At N = 2,000, we selected default-start fits in which the block means differed in magnitude by more than .10 (|M | > .1). Below the continuous-ML threshold, 93% of selected continuous-ML fits favored the first-listed block. At or above the threshold, 53% did. The corresponding percentages below and at or above each estimator's threshold were 93% and 50% for ML on ordinal scores, 77% and 53% for ULS, and 64% and 51% for WLSMV. This preference for the first block is consistent with lavaan's default starting loadings. Figure 4 gives the pooled proportions and Appendix G.5 gives the counts.

7 An Illustration Based on Published PHQ-ADS Results

Kroenke

The calculation assumes an exactly fitting two-factor population with the two-factor loadings reported by Kroenke et al. (2016, Supplemental Digital Content, Table S3). The sensitivity calculation replaces these loadings by a common loading between .70 and .80. Neither calculation is a reconstruction of the trial-specific fits. There is also an estimator difference: the published analysis treated the responses as ordered categorical in Mplus with a logistic link, whereas the population calculation applies normal-theory ML and treats the published standardized loadings as latent-response loadings. Categorical estimation can change the fit indices (Lubbe, 2023). Finally, the reported two-factor RMSEA exceeded .06 in all three trials. The population calculation therefore isolates the discrepancy due to merging the two traits under the stated assumptions; it does not allocate the observed misfit between omitted dimensionality and other sources.

The illustration shows three substantively different patterns (Table 5). At INCPAD's correlation of approximately .65, the one-factor population with the published loadings has RMSEA .122 and CFI .803, and the common-loading range gives RMSEA from .10 to .15 and CFI from .80 to .84.

These values are of similar magnitude to the reported .130 and .862 and show that merging traits can itself produce substantial misfit in this range. At ESCAPE's correlation of .865, the published loadings give CFI = .951 but RMSEA = .065, the same kind of disagreement between conventional cutoffs that ESCAPE reported; a common loading near .75 gives CFI = .953 and RMSEA = .065. At SCOPE's correlation of .912, population RMSEA is .058 with the published loadings and ranges from .037 to .060 with a common loading (.0602 at loading .80, marginally above the cutoff), and CFI exceeds .96 in both calculations. The reported RMSEA is .091 for one factor and .085 for two factors, so failure of the one-factor RMSEA cutoff alone cannot attribute the discrepancy to merging depression and anxiety.

The disagreement between CFI and RMSEA follows from their different denominators. For this 16-item one-factor model, RMSEA divides the discrepancy by 104 degrees of freedom and meets .06 only when F min ≤ .06 2 ×104 ≈ .374. CFI divides the same discrepancy by the independence-model discrepancy, which is 8.9 at ESCAPE's correlation with the published ESCAPE loadings. With these loadings, CFI reaches .95 from a trait correlation of approximately .864 and RMSEA reaches .06 from approximately .878, so ESCAPE's correlation of .865 lies just inside the interval in which the two cutoffs disagree. In the common-loading sensitivity calculation at φ = .865, the independence-model discrepancy is 7.3 for a common loading of .70, 9.4 for .75, and 12.0 for .80. With loading .70, the one-factor model meets both cutoffs from a correlation of approximately .84. With loading .75, the CFI threshold is .86 and the RMSEA threshold is .88; with loading .80, the disagreement interval

The corresponding depression shares in regression or Bartlett scores are .57 to .58 and .63 to .68, compared with 9/16 = .56 in the unit-weighted sum score. With the published two-factor loadings, depression receives the larger coefficient share only in ESCAPE. In all three trials the anxiety items have higher two-factor loadings on average than the depression items, with block means of .72 and .80 in SCOPE, .71 and .75 in ESCAPE, and .66 and .75 in INCPAD, and the population one-factor approximation gives depression a coefficient share of .46, .53 and .33. When the blocks differ in length, the higher loadings alone do not determine which trait the factor favors (Section 5.2). The anxiety block has the larger total correlation in SCOPE (2.43 against 2.39) and INCPAD (2.02 against 1.70), whereas in ESCAPE the smaller loading difference leaves the larger total correlation with the longer depression block (2.13 against 1.81). With one summary loading per block, the that applies as φ approaches 1 orders the blocks in the same way, and in these calculations the favored block is the same at every trait correlation.

The one-factor loadings implied by the published two-factor solutions agree closely with the published one-factor loadings: across the 16 items their correlations are 1.000, .999 and .961. With the published two-factor loadings as reference, the published one-factor loadings give depression coefficient shares of .46, .51 and .44. At INCPAD's correlation the regression factor score correlates .81 with depression and .94 with anxiety, whereas the unit-weighted sum correlates .89 and .87.

The factor share and score share are distinct quantities, and the factor score and the sum score represent the two traits differently.

These results establish the behavior of the specified population model, not the composition of the published PHQ-ADS scores. The published loadings are estimates from a categorical model, and the reported samples add sampling uncertainty; for example, ESCAPE had n = 241 and sample RMSEA .083 with 104 degrees of freedom. The finite-sample study provides relevant design-based context, but neither that study nor this illustration removes the estimator difference or the misspecification of the published two-factor model.

8 Discussion

Consider four items, two per trait, with loadings of .50. When the traits are uncorrelated, either optimal one-factor ML solution reproduces one block exactly and assigns zero loadings to the other.

Its population SRMR is .079, just below the conventional cutoff of .08. A one-factor model can therefore meet this cutoff even when the fitted factor represents only one of the two traits.

8.1 Interpreting One-Factor Fit

The CFI cutoff gives a different result in these designs. Every CFI boundary in Table 1 lies above the ML transition, where the fitted factor represents both traits equally. With unequal blocks, the global solution can favor one trait even at high correlations, and a second local minimum can favor the other. Fit indices alone cannot identify which trait receives the larger weight.

For a proposed item structure, an analyst can calculate the trait correlation at which the one-factor model meets a conventional cutoff and repeat the calculation over plausible loadings. This is particularly relevant when a well-fitting merged model is taken as evidence against discriminant validity (Rönkkö & Cho, 2022). Dynamic fit indices for one-factor models use residual correlations as a source of misspecification (McNeish & Wolf, 2023). Groskurth et al. (2025) allow a two-factor alternative and select cutoffs from simulated classification performance. Here the cutoff is fixed, and the calculation identifies the population correlations compatible with it. Finite-sample error rates require a separate analysis.

To interpret the fitted factor, we need both the one-factor loadings and the loadings in the proposed two-trait model. The composition of an estimated factor must also be distinguished from that of a score computed from the items: regression and Bartlett factor scores have the same relative trait contributions in the setting considered here, but these generally differ from those of the fitted factor and the unit-weighted sum. Reporting one score therefore requires an interpretation of that score's weights as well as an assessment of model fit. ML, unweighted least squares, and principal components can represent different directions for the same population correlation matrix, so the estimation criterion matters beyond standard errors and goodness-of-fit corrections. Likewise, the close agreement of lavaan's robust categorical indices (Savalei, 2021) with the continuous-ML references near the cutoffs is a numerical result for the studied designs and does not identify the categorical fitted factor with the ML fitted factor.

8.2 Computation and Reporting

In the simulations, the default fit more often favored the trait whose items were listed first. When the blocks differed, it was also associated with whether that solution had a higher objective value and favored the weaker block. Both associations are consistent with lavaan's default starting values, which are anchored on the first-listed item (Section 6). For a one-factor model fitted to known item blocks, a useful check is therefore to compare the solutions obtained with each block listed first and with additional starting values, retaining the discrepancy and loading pattern of each distinct solution. The archived multistart results support this check for the studied designs (Section 6) but do not prove that two orders are sufficient in general. In the population refits, different identifications led to different solutions from the same starting covariance. One reported convergence was at a symmetric saddle. When competing solutions affect interpretation, objective comparisons should be accompanied by checks of the relevant first-and second-order conditions.

For a one-factor ML model with nonnegative uniquenesses, the boundary criterion of Proposition 4 (Appendix B) gives a necessary condition for a solution with one zero uniqueness to be a local minimum. In the two-trait population it excludes such minima except at the stated two-item, zero-correlation endpoint; more generally, it can rule out a reported zero-uniqueness solution when releasing that uniqueness decreases the discrepancy. The result does not classify unconstrained negative uniqueness estimates or solutions obtained by other estimators.

The R package undeRfactor (Tomašević, 2026b) computes ML, ULS, and WLSMV thresholds with phi_star() and ML cutoff boundaries with blind_spot(). For 0 < φ < 1 and one population loading per block, block_solutions() uses the quartic in Appendix D.2 to find the positive blockuniform stationary points. These include every local minimum up to a common sign. The package also compares numerical candidates and item orders, computes factor and score shares, and fits the one-factor model implied by an estimated two-factor model (predict_one_factor()). Where numerical search is required, it reports the distinct candidates found. Signed coefficient shares depend on trait orientation and require a nonzero coefficient sum. The coefficients themselves require nonzero mean reference loadings in both blocks and |φ| < 1.

8.3 Scope and Further Work

The exact results concern a structured two-trait population. The exchangeable case permits a closed global solution, and constant loadings within unequal blocks permit an exact reduction to a quartic equation. For unequal block lengths, this reduction gives a selection rule but not a closed partition of the full design space, and the global solution need not vary continuously with the trait correlation (Section 5.2). For loadings that vary within blocks, the general information-loss bound (Appendix E) and numerical examples provide partial results. Independent residuals are part of the generating model, and more than two traits are outside the present analysis. Matching lower bounds for variable loadings, a full classification of competing minima with unequal block lengths, and extensions to more than two traits are therefore priorities for further analytic work.

The ML theorems describe the population discrepancy. The simulations cover sample sizes from 250 to 2,000 in the specified continuous and ordinal designs. The study does not establish performance for smaller samples, nonnormal continuous responses, or every set of ordinal thresholds; in particular, different item thresholds generally remove the two-weight structure used in the weighted least-squares result. Archived solution groups identify alternatives found by the specified starts but do not certify sample stationarity or global optimality. The power summaries use conventional noncentral-χ 2 approximations; their finite-sample accuracy, especially near the transition and at nonregular endpoints, was not assessed.

Equal cross-loadings yield an exact transformation of the latent-response covariance into the two-block form. The Gaussian analogue of the Strachan et al. (2022) design suggests a mechanism for their reported instability at negative correlations but is not a replication of binary marginal-ML estimation, and the binary calculations (Appendix H) provide numerical evidence rather than a general theorem for IRT models. Likewise, the PHQ-ADS illustration applies normal-theory ML to the published two-factor loadings, which were estimated from ordered categorical responses with a logistic link, and uses a common-loading range of .70 to .80 as a sensitivity analysis. It is therefore not an exact reanalysis of the original categorical responses and cannot by itself validate the total score.

The exchangeable two-trait population with φ ≥ 0 also admits a symmetric bifactor representation, with general loadings λ √ φ and specific loadings λ √ 1 -φ. In this representation, explained common variance equals φ. Each threshold therefore also gives a value of this index of essential unidimensionality (Reise et al., 2013; Rodriguez et al., 2016).

For a scale intended to measure both traits, report the fitted loadings by block and the weights used to construct the score. Two solutions can have identical fit and give most of their weight to different traits.

A.4 Completion of the Proof for Positive Trait Correlation

Let 0 < φ < 1. By Lemma A.1 a global minimum exists, and it is a local minimum. By Lemmas A.4-A.6 every local minimum has block-uniform positive uniquenesses. Its discrepancy is therefore at least H(d) for its value of d (Lemma A.7), and hence at least the minimum of H. That minimum is attained by feasible points. The global minimizers are therefore the points of Lemma A.8 with the scale of Lemma A.7 and the concentrated loading: one covariance when φ ≥ φ * , including equality, and two covariances, exchanged by the interchange of the blocks, when φ < φ *.

Every local minimum is one of these. For each d, let Ψ(d) be the block-uniform uniquenesses with e s = Q(d)/ν, and let l(d) be the positive concentrated loading of Lemma A.2. For φ > 0 the leading eigenvalue of the whitened matrix is simple. A simple eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix that depends smoothly on a parameter has a smooth eigenvector, by the implicit function theorem applied to the eigenvalue equation with a normalization. Hence (l(d), Ψ(d)) is a smooth curve of feasible points, and F (l(d), Ψ(d)) = H(d) along it. Consider a local minimum, with uniquenesses given by (s, d). It is a nonzero local minimum over the loadings, so by Lemma A.2 its loading is the concentrated one and its leading whitened eigenvalue exceeds one. Near this scale the concentrated loading is continuous in s, and the concentrated discrepancy is strictly convex in s (Lemma A.7); a local minimum therefore has e s = Q(d)/ν. It lies on the curve, and d is a local minimum of H. By Lemma A.8, H has no local minimum other than its global ones. This excludes additional local minima of the full problem for φ > 0. Every covariance obtained in this way has nonzero off-diagonal entries, and l 2 i = Σ ij Σ ik /Σ jk for distinct i, j, k. The loadings are therefore determined by the covariance up to a common sign; parameter nonuniqueness occurs only in the two-item endpoint family at φ = 0.

The boundary covariance Σ ⋆ is obtained by regressing every other item on item j and treating the resulting residuals as independent. A negative derivative indicates residual covariance that can be represented by moving into the interior of the one-factor model. In the exchangeable two-trait population, the derivative is strictly negative except at m = 2 and φ = 0; Lemma A.5 evaluates the sum. At that endpoint, boundary representations occur in the exact-fit family for the retained pair.

For an observed zero-uniqueness ML solution, the covariance form and derivative provide necessary checks for a local minimum. If the covariance is Σ ⋆ and the derivative is strictly positive, the solution is a strict local minimum of the discrepancy over the loadings and uniquenesses.

C.6 Weights for WLSMV

For the WLSMV calculations, the residual weights are inverse asymptotic variances of two-step polychoric estimates. We obtained them from the estimator's influence function, including estimation of the item thresholds, by numerical differentiation of bivariate normal cell probabilities. The resulting population weights agree with lavaan's estimated asymptotic covariance matrix for 200,000 cases to within 0.3%. The implementation is included in the supplementary code.

First, a symmetric matrix with a nonsingular leading block is congruent to the block-diagonal matrix formed by that block and its Schur complement, so its numbers of positive, negative and zero eigenvalues are the sums of theirs (Haynsworth's inertia additivity). Second, if f (x, y) has a smooth family of stationary points x(y) in x with nonsingular f xx , the Hessian of the concentrated function f (x(y), y) is the Schur complement f yy -f yx f -1 xx f xy . Classification. For 0 < φ < 1, by Lemma 1, every local minimum of the unrestricted problem is a stationary point of the kind in Lemma D.4(ii). The optimal scale is continuous in d because Q AB (d) > 0 is continuous, and the positive leading eigenvector varies continuously because the leading eigenvalue is simple. Along the resulting feasible curve of Lemma D.3, indexed by d, the discrepancy equals G(d), so a local minimum corresponds to a positive root that is a local minimum of G. Conversely, by Lemma D.5, a simple root that is a minimum of G gives a positive-definite Hessian and hence a strict local minimum of the unrestricted problem, and a simple root that is a maximum of G gives a saddle with exactly one negative Hessian eigenvalue. Away from repeated roots there is therefore either one local minimum, or two local minima separated by a saddle. A global minimum exists (Lemma A.1) and is found by comparing (D.1) at the one or two minimum roots. When two minima have equal profile values, both are global and the minimizing covariance is not unique. A numerical solution of the exact quartic finds such an equal-value point in the second unequal-size example of Section 5.2 (Appendix D.5), and the global solution changes discontinuously there; this is a numerical result, not a proved one. For equal block sizes with unequal loadings, Proposition 2 excludes tied global minima; with equal loadings, Theorem 1 gives the tied pair of block-reflected minima for 0 < φ < φ *.

A double positive root has a cubic leading term in the local profile, so the discrepancy decreases along the curve on one side and the point is not a local minimum. At a nondegenerate fold it coexists with a separate simple minimum. A triple positive root v 0 is the only positive root: with ϱ > 0 and v -< 0, the derivative identity gives a positive quartic leading term in G -G(v 0 ), and the point is the global minimum, with one zero Hessian eigenvalue.

The exchangeable threshold is such a triple-root case. A positive root of multiplicity four is impossible because P has a negative root. A fold as φ varies requires and nondegeneracy additionally requires P vv ̸ = 0 and P φ ̸ = 0.

A vanishing resultant alone is not sufficient to identify a feasible fold.

These statements classify all positive block-uniform stationary points and, by Lemma 1, all local minima. They do not enumerate zero-loading or sign-changing saddles of the unrestricted likelihood.

For arbitrary unequal sizes, they give an exact root-comparison procedure rather than a closed partition of the entire parameter space.

D.4 Mirrored Heterogeneous Loadings

If both blocks contain the same set of nonconstant loadings, simultaneous exchange of corresponding items preserves the population covariance. Such a design retains the block-exchange symmetry, but Lemma 1 no longer applies because the items within a block are not exchangeable. We compute the curvature along perturbations that distinguish the two blocks. Data Availability

The code, archived simulation summaries, portable evidence files and the supporting proofs (Online Resources 1-3, materials release 1.2) are available at https://github.com/atomashevic/one-factor-two-traits and archived at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24337803). The R package undeRfactor, version 0.2.0, which implements the population calculations, is available at https://github.com/atomashevic/undeRfactor and archived at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23668208). The raw output of the 2.3 million model fits in the simulation study is not included in the repository and is available from the author on request. No new empirical data were collected for this article; the PHQ-ADS illustration is based on published results.

G.1 Design and Objectives

The study had four objectives. The first was to compare sample CFI, TLI, RMSEA and SRMR with their population values and to determine how often the one-factor model meets conventional cutoffs. The second was to examine the size and direction of loading imbalance, including whether averaging across replications obscures solutions that favor different traits. The third was to assess whether initial values return higher-objective solutions that favor the weaker block. The fourth was to examine these patterns under categorical estimation.

The design crossed 92 populations, four sample sizes (250, 500, 1,000 and 2,000), and three response formats, yielding 1,104 cells. We generated 1,000 replications per continuous cell and 500 per ordinal cell. Ordinal responses had four categories. Symmetric thresholds were -.8, 0 flag marks a fitted factor that follows the trait of the weaker block.

G.2 Population Reference Points

The ML thresholds in Design A were .25 and .20 for loading .5 with m = 4 and 8, respectively, and .41 and .37 for loading .7. Design B used .41 as an exchangeable reference at the mean loading; unequal loading blocks do not have a symmetric solution. Design C likewise has no symmetric solution because its block lengths differ. The additional low-correlation grid points in Design A were chosen to cover estimator-specific thresholds.

For ULS, the population threshold is 1/p. WLSMV fits polychoric correlations by weighted least squares, with each correlation weighted by its inverse asymptotic variance. Let ω be the ratio of cross-block to within-block weights. For ω > (m -1)/m, Proposition 1 places the transition at φ ω in equation (5.1), below which the symmetric solution ceases to be the global minimizer; φ ω reduces to 1/p when ω = 1. In the evaluated exchangeable ordinal designs, within-block correlations were estimated more precisely, giving ω < 1 and the lower WLSMV thresholds reported in Section 5.1.

At m = 4 and loading .5, these were approximately .08: .081 for symmetric categories and .076 for skewed categories. For Design B, the weaker-block minimum exists below the documented folds φ f = .242 for loadings .68 and .72, and .017 for loadings .60 and .80.

The second study objective also had an asymptotic motivation. In Gaussian spiked-covariance models with identity noise, as dimension and sample size grow proportionally, a spectral transition occurs at spike excess p/N (Baik et al., 2005; Paul, 2007). Comparing κ -with this scale provides a heuristic for dependence on N and φ. It is not a finite-sample detection boundary for the loading contrasts used here.

G.3 Numerical Conventions and Retained Evidence

Population continuous-ML references were obtained by multistart fitting, are reported as the best solutions found, and were checked against the closed forms where they apply. Population ML on scores used the exact score covariance matrix. For WLSMV, the DWLS correlation weights were computed numerically from the influence function at the true polychoric correlations and thresholds. The full asymptotic covariance matrix used for the corrections was estimated from 200,000 generated observations, and reference fit indices were evaluated at nominal N = 1,000,000.

Thus, the WLSMV reference calculation combines analytic population inputs with numerically estimated correction ingredients. We distinguish unscaled WLSMV indices, scaled indices based on scale-and-shift adjusted test statistics, and robust categorical indices based on a normal-theory discrepancy at the DWLS estimates with separate corrections (Savalei, 2021).

All simulation fits, including the multistart refits, were run in R 4.5.1 (R Core Team, 2025) with lavaan 0.6-20 (Rosseel, 2012), the versions recorded in the archived output; the controls in Appendix G.6 used R 4.6.1 and lavaan 0.7-2. The simulation required approximately 150 CPU hours for 2.3 million fits (one-factor and two-factor fits; ULS was fitted with the one-factor model only; the multistart refits in Designs B and C are additional). One seed per population and sample size was shared by the three response formats: the cell seed was 100,000 k + 10,000 j for population k and the jth sample size (j = 1, . . . , 4 for N = 250, 500, 1,000 and 2,000), and replication r used the cell seed plus r. No replication returned an error. All 1.21 million one-factor fits reported convergence; among the 1.10 million two-factor fits, nonconvergence was at most 0.2% (1 of 500) in any cell, and 33 had a negative estimated uniqueness. Of the one-factor fits, seven had negative estimated uniquenesses: six ML fits to ordinal scores and one WLSMV fit. These unconstrained negative estimates are outside the zero-uniqueness ML boundary classification. The archived summaries retain them and also give the subset with positive recorded uniquenesses. None occurs in the N = 2,000 subsets used in Figures 3 and 4.

All one-factor fits, in the primary runs and in the multistart refits, fixed the factor variance at 1 (std.lv = TRUE) and, unless random starts are named, used lavaan's default starting values; marker-variable identification was used only in the controls of Appendix G.6. Regenerating five replications of each of four archived cells, and all replications of the 18 continuous cells behind Table 4, from their seeds with the deposited code under R 4.5.1 and lavaan 0.6-20 reproduced the archived objective and CFI exactly. Under this identification, lavaan's default starting loadings depended on item order: in the two cells inspected, with either version of lavaan, they were close to the generating loading for the first-listed block and lower for the other block (about 0 at φ = 0). For multistart fitting in Designs B and C, each fit used the two default item orders and 20 random starts, with loadings sampled uniformly on (0, 1) and uniquenesses uniformly on (.2, 1). Reported-converged solutions were grouped at standardized-loading tolerance .002. The lowest objective in each group was retained, and groups were compared at tolerance 10 -7 in lavaan's objective. The archive does not retain the objective from every individual start. A positive recorded uniqueness, reported convergence, or agreement with the lowest observed objective does not establish stationarity or global optimality.

Stationarity was checked afterwards for the 18 combinations of population and sample size in Table 4. Their 18,000 replications were regenerated from the seeds with the deposited code under R 4.5.1 and lavaan 0.6-20, keeping every start. The regenerated default-start objective and CFI, the lowest objective and the group flags equaled the archived values in every replication. For each retained group, the analytic gradient and Hessian of the ML discrepancy F , as a function of the loadings and uniquenesses, were evaluated at the group's estimate with the lowest objective, with the tolerances of Appendix G.6: a strict local minimum required a largest absolute gradient element of at most 10 -6 and a smallest Hessian eigenvalue above 10 -5 . Above the population fold (loadings .68 and .72, φ = .3), of the 262 higher-objective weaker-block groups at N = 500, 129 met both conditions at the lavaan estimate. The other 133 exceeded the gradient tolerance, by a largest value of 8.0 × 10 -6 , and met both conditions after Newton steps that changed no standardized loading by more than 2.4 × 10 -6 . At N = 2,000 the corresponding counts were 26 and 43 of 69, with largest gradient 5.2 × 10 -6 and largest change 9.5 × 10 -6 . The smallest Hessian eigenvalue in these groups was .013 at N = 500 and .025 at N = 2,000. Over all 18 combinations, 11,464 replications had a higher-objective weaker-block group; 2,217 of these groups met both conditions at the lavaan estimate and the other 9,247 after Newton steps, with smallest Hessian eigenvalue .006. The same held for all 29,649 retained groups (10,862 at the lavaan estimate), including the best group found in each replication; none was a saddle. The largest gradient element at a lavaan estimate was 2.7 × 10 -5 , and no Newton refinement changed a standardized loading by more than 1.7 × 10 -5 . Each retained group of Table 4, including the higher-objective weaker-block groups above the population fold, therefore lies at a strict local minimum of the sample discrepancy or within 1.7 × 10 -5 of one in every standardized loading. This check concerns local minima of those sample objectives; it does not establish that the best group found is a global minimum.

For Table 4, default and best-found fits were paired within replication. For ML, lavaan's objective is fx = F/2. The estimated baseline noncentrality was reconstructed as

Best-found CFI used T best = 2N fx best and the standard nonnegative truncations,

The inversion requires 0 < CFI default < 1, equivalently 0 < T -df < B. It was satisfied by all 18,000 pairs of Table 4 (nine rows, two sample sizes and 1,000 replications). The accompanying evidence contains the paired terms, selected fit rows, figure exports and calculation scripts. The population calculations are also implemented in the accompanying R package undeRfactor (version 0.2.0, https://github.com/atomashevic/undeRfactor).

G.4 Further Results on Fit Indices

The agreement between sample fit indices and their population references depended on the solution returned. In Designs B and C, mean CFI at the best solution found differed from its population value by at most .004 at N = 500 and .0013 at N = 2,000; the corresponding differences for RMSEA were .0023 and .0006. In Design A with four items per trait and loading .5 (default starts), mean CFI exceeded its population value by about .05 throughout φ ≤ φ * at N = 250 (maximum .056).

At N = 1,000 and 2,000 the bias peaked at φ = .2, just below φ * = .25 (.019 and .016). This peak near the threshold at the larger sample sizes is consistent with the small curvature in the direction that differentiates the blocks. Because these population CFI values are below .62, the bias does not affect cutoff decisions in this range. RMSEA remained within .003 of its population value at N ≥ 1,000. At N = 250, the upward bias of SRMR reached .03. The sample and population half-pass correlations compared in Section 6 were both located by linear interpolation between evaluated correlations, which are spaced .1 apart outside the added points. The cutoff-passing comparison at φ = .912 reported there used skewed four-category items for WLSMV (Figure 5).

The robust WLSMV comparison in Section 6 covers the evaluated populations with φ ≥ .7, which included every evaluated population meeting continuous-ML CFI ≥ .95. At lower correlations, INCPAD ESCAPE SCOPE .5 .6 .7 .8 .9 Trait correlation ' 0% 25% 50% 75% 100% Samples meeting the cutoff CFI ¸: 95 INCPAD ESCAPE SCOPE .5 .6 .7 .8 .9 Trait correlation ' RMSEA • : 06 ML, continuous items WLSMV, robust WLSMV, scaled WLSMV, unscaled robust CFI could be lower, and WLSMV could retain a composite solution where ML produced unequal block loadings.

Unscaled and scaled WLSMV indices were more lenient in the near-cutoff comparisons. Figure 5 shows the PHQ-ADS layout with skewed four-category items at N = 250. At INCPAD's correlation, unscaled WLSMV CFI met .95 in 92% of samples and scaled CFI did so in 1%; neither continuous ML nor robust WLSMV CFI met the cutoff.

At ESCAPE's correlation of .865, CFI and RMSEA often gave different decisions. CFI passed in 57% of continuous-ML samples and 42% of robust WLSMV samples, whereas RMSEA passed in 26% and 21%, respectively; scaled CFI passed in 99%. Section 6 reports the comparison at SCOPE's correlation of .912.

G.5 Further Results on Loading Imbalance and Item Order

In the setting of Figure 3, mean |C mag | under ML was .500 at φ = .2. Under ULS, it was .834 at 0, .317 at its population threshold 1/p = .125, .117 at .2 and .050 at .3; under WLSMV on symmetric categories, it was .037 at .2.

The unnormalized magnitude contrast showed both close agreement with the population result and attenuation at smaller sample sizes. With four items per trait, loading .7 and N = 2,000, mean |M | under ML at φ = .2 was .458, compared with .459 in the population. With four items per trait, loading .5 and N = 250, it was .412 at φ = 0, compared with .50 in the population. These continuous summaries describe the amount of imbalance without treating a reference distribution at one correlation as a test at another.

The effect of averaging depended on both estimator and sign convention. For continuous ML at φ = 0, with four items per trait, loading .7 and N = 2,000, all 1,000 fits favored the first-listed block: its mean loading lA lay between .669 and .724, and lB between -.100 and.

101. No fit required a common sign change, so D > 0 in every fit, and mean D and mean |D| were both .701. The 510 fits with opposite block signs are those in which the near-zero lB was negative; for them |D| > |M |, and mean |M | was .674. Averaging D therefore did not obscure the imbalance in this cell, because the default start selected the same block in every replication. Under ULS, averaging did obscure imbalance: at its population threshold, the mean signed difference was .02 and the mean absolute difference was .30. The directional proportions of Section 6 separate two regimes. A cell is below the threshold of an estimator when the population solution of that estimator has unequal block loadings: φ < φ * for continuous ML, φ < 1/p for ULS, and, for ML on scores and WLSMV, a best population solution found whose block loadings differ by more than .005 (the same cells are selected with any tolerance from .001 to .01); threshold equality counts as the composite regime. At N = 2,000, the first-block/selected counts below the threshold were 22,125/23,714 (continuous ML, 24 of the 53 population cells), 10,221/10,934 (ML on scores, 22 cells), 8,391/10,842 (ULS, 11 cells) and 1,169/1,835 (WLSMV, 4 cells). At or above the threshold they were 2,642/5,005, 1,287/2,567, 3,994/7,502 and 1,480/2,911. The pooled counts over all 53 cells were 24,767/28,719, 11,508/13,501, 12,385/18,344 and 2,649/4,746.

At φ = 0 alone, the counts were 3,999/4,000, 1,998/2,000, 3,534/3,994 and 736/1,206. The ordinal analyses used symmetric categories. Below the threshold the two population minima are mirror images, so the first-block proportions there reflect the starting values; at or above it the population solution is a composite, and a selected fit is a sampling departure from that solution. Pooled over all cells, 86% of selected continuous-ML fits favored the first-listed block at N = 2,000, compared with 74% at N = 250; below the threshold the proportions were 93% and 83%.

With the weaker block listed first, continuous ML returned a higher-objective group favoring that block in 27 to 45% of samples with loadings .60 and .80 at φ ≤ .01, for N = 500 and 2,000, compared with 94 to 100% for loadings .68 and .72 at φ ≤ .1. With loadings .68 and .72, φ = 0 and N = 2,000, the default fit gave CFI = .44 and RMSEA = .250, compared with .56 and .223 at the best solution found, and the default factor favored the trait with lower generating loadings.

Listing the weaker block last produced no weaker-block flags in any of the 234 archived cell-analysis combinations (78 population-sample-size cells × three ML analyses). Because none of the 761 replications that retained a higher-objective group under the weaker-last order had a weaker-block flag, a higher objective and a weaker-block loading pattern are distinct properties. With loadings .68 and .72 at φ = .3, above the population fold, higher-objective weaker-block groups occurred in 26% of default fits at N = 500 and 7% at N = 2,000. Across cells, the largest mean recorded fraction of converged random starts assigned to the selected higher-objective weaker-block group was 36%, in a cell analyzed by ML on ordinal scores (35.5% for continuous ML).

G.6 Starting Covariance and Identification Controls

Equal starting covariances did not imply equal optimization paths. Six population cases were refitted under two item orders and two identifications, using default starts and a common starting covariance (R 4.6.1, lavaan 0.7-2). The 48 fits included 47 reported convergences. Gradient and Hessian checks supported 39 strict local minima and identified two saddles; seven fits exceeded the gradient tolerance of 10 -6 . Evidence for a strict local minimum additionally required a smallest Hessian eigenvalue above 10 -5.

The common starting covariance used loadings .6 and uniquenesses .64 under unit latent variance.

In the unequal-loading cases, all 20 common-start fits agreed with the best numerical reference objective within 3.8 × 10 -11 . Four exceeded the gradient tolerance, including one nonconverged fit, so objective agreement did not verify every fit as a minimum. In the exchangeable case with loading .7 and φ = .3, unit-variance identification reached the symmetric saddle, with F = .970752 and smallest Hessian eigenvalue -.306480. Marker identification reached either analytic global minimum, with F = .940795, depending on item order.

G.7 Assessment of the Study Predictions

Four predictions were stated with the design, and a fifth was added after the pilot from the categorical weighted-least-squares result. The first predicted that mean CFI and RMSEA for continuous ML would be within .01 of their population values at N ≥ 1,000. For Designs B and C at the best solution found, and for Design A at the default solution, RMSEA met this prediction in every evaluated cell. CFI did so except in Design A with loading .5 near φ * , where the default-start difference reached .019 at N = 1,000. Higher-objective default solutions below the fold lowered CFI by as much as .23.

The second prediction was that exchangeable designs would favor the two blocks about equally often, causing mean loadings to resemble a composite. The directional summaries did not support equal selection under the default ML start: below each estimator's population threshold, conditional first-block proportions at N = 2,000 were 93% for ML, 93% for ML on scores, 77% for ULS and 64% for WLSMV (86%, 85%, 68% and 56% pooled over all correlations). The ordinal summaries used symmetric categories and selection required |M | > .1.

The third prediction was that unequal-loading designs would favor the stronger block and that weaker-block minima would occur essentially below φ f . The best solutions found supported the stronger-block prediction. Higher-objective groups favoring the weaker block also occurred above the population fold; in the two cells at φ = .3 all 331 lay at, or within 10 -5 in every standardized loading of, strict local minima of the sample discrepancy (Appendix G.3), so sample minima of this kind are not confined to correlations below φ f.

The fourth prediction placed the ULS transition at 1/p, below the ML threshold. Sample imbalance decreased across this point without disappearing. At N = 2,000, mean |C mag | was .117 at φ = .2 and .050 at .3 for ULS, compared with .500 and .312 for ML. The fifth prediction related WLSMV imbalance to its own population threshold. With four items per trait and loading .7, the population solution remained a composite; sample mean |C mag | was .102 at φ = 0 and .037 at .2 for symmetric categories and N = 2,000. The diagnostics describe magnitude and polarity separately and do not define a false-positive rate by calibration at another correlation.

H Binary Responses

The transition from a factor favoring one trait to a factor representing both traits also appeared in population computations for binary items. We considered four normal-ogive items, two per trait, with slopes corresponding to a loading of .7. The population distribution was evaluated over all 2 p response patterns, and a one-trait model was fitted by minimizing KL divergence with multiple starts and 41 to 121 Gauss-Hermite nodes; the fits reported below are the best solutions found.

The ratio 1 -KL / TC, termed information CFI, extends the population CFI interpretation to this response format.

With the thresholds b in P (X = 1 | θ) = Φ(aθ -b) fixed at 0 and φ = 0, the best-found fit had slopes 0 in one block and .98 in the other. The information loss was 0.0781 bits, equal to the mutual information within the ignored block, at each of 41, 81 and 121 quadrature nodes. At φ = .2, .3 and .35, the favored and other block slopes were .94 and .23, .87 and .37, and .80 and .47, respectively. At φ = .4, the slopes were equal. At high trait correlations, little response information distinguished the two-trait model from its one-trait approximation. Define the signed contrast D = lA -lB , the magnitude contrast M = | lA | -| lB |, and the normalized magnitude contrastC mag = | lA |/λ ref A -| lB |/λ ref B | lA |/λ ref A + | lB |/λ ref B ,whereλ ref A , λ ref B >0 are reference block loadings and the denominator must be positive. The references are the generating loadings for continuous ML, ULS and WLSMV, and the stored population scorescale loadings for ML on scores. We report mean |C mag |, mean |M |, and the frequency of opposite block signs. These quantities describe loading patterns; they are not factor-score estimates. The directional proportions of Section 6, which count fits with M > .1 among those with |M | > .1, are conditional on selection and are undefined when no fit is selected. The separate weaker-block flag used in the multistart archive compares reference-normalized magnitudes, | lA |/λ ref A and | lB |/λ ref B , for the population-designated weaker block; it does not use the .1 cutoff. The weaker block is the block with the lower loading in Design B, which is listed first, and the 7-item block in Design C. The information loss was almost entirely residual local dependence. Let P (x) denote the population distribution of the response patterns and Q the fitted one-trait model, with trait density π(η), item response functions Q(x i | η) and posterior Q(η | x). Couple the two through the joint law P (x, η) = P (x) Q(η | x), with trait marginal P (η) and conditionals P (x | η) and P (x i | η). Because P and Q have the same posterior, KL(P ∥ Q) equals the divergence between the two joint laws, and KL(P ∥ Q) = E P (η) KL P (x | η) i P (x i | η)
